verdict: This is a genuinely good French deck in its judgement and a poor one in its housekeeping. The sociolinguistic calls are better than most published courses: on over nous at tier 1, ne-drop taught as a listening skill rather than a footnote, question words parked at the end (t'es où ?, c'est quoi ?), n'est-ce pas explicitly killed off, the partitive promoted to day one, merci-alone flagged as a refusal, the je suis plein trap headed off, tenez versus voilà, saignant/à point/bien cuit put where 'not too spicy' used to sit, and the tu/vous negotiation taught as a spoken event. Against that sit three structural defects. First, deduplication never happened: roughly sixty pairs repeat, and dozens carry conflicting tiers, so the scheduler will teach la baguette, faire la bise and les parents at both tier 1 and tier 2, épicé at both 3 and 4, and la route, le portable, les infos, commencer, allumer, tu me manques, je me suis fait mal, en face, le métro, la famille and chez two or three times each. Second, about forty notes still explain French by reference to Hindi (dal, ghee, khichdi, biryani, raita, nimbu paani, sari, jaldi, zara, parson, lakh and crore, touching an elder's feet, taking your shoes off), which is meaningless to a British learner and occasionally wrong, as with the sala comparison at hs-0834 and the garbled leftovers at hs-0014, hs-0015 and hs-1073. Third, three N/A slots (hs-0568, hs-0726, hs-0751) are dead placeholders that duplicate live items, and one of them is factually false: French does have both une coupure de courant and y a plus de courant, and it has native/loanword doublets all over the place. The tier curve is also still Hindi-shaped at the top: rice, pasta and salt sit at tier 1 while vouloir sits at 2 and the pronoun en at 3, behind four tier-2 chunks that depend on it. The coverage holes are the most serious finding, because they are things the spine could not have known to ask for: the affirmative il y a is absent although il y a pas is tier 1; there is no ce/cette/ces, no rule for the definite article where English drops it, no ne...plus, no est-ce que, no reflexive pronoun paradigm and nothing at all on liaison; voilà, salut, bonsoir, de rien, du coup, vraiment, sympa and pas mal exist only inside other items' notes; payer, rentrer, trouver and un rendez-vous are missing outright; the restaurant sequence has no entrée/plat/dessert, no table booking, no beer and no service compris; there is no boulangerie, no aller-retour, nothing for driving (se garer, le péage, l'essence) and almost nothing for sightseeing; and the single most useful direction question in the language, pour aller à la gare, s'il vous plaît ?, appears only as a parenthesis under pour. One last data note: the roman field is meaningless for a Latin-script language and is applied inconsistently anyway, accent-stripped up to hs-0385 and verbatim thereafter, so it should either mirror the word or be dropped. Fix the duplicates, run a de-Hindi pass over the notes, and fold in the additions below, and this becomes a real French curriculum rather than a well-translated Hindi one.

items.note: il est / elle est / c'est. c'est is the one you'll say most.
'not' is a separate machine: (ne) ... pas, wrapped round the verb.
si is the special yes that contradicts a negative: – Tu viens pas ? – Si !
j' before a vowel: j'ai, j'aime.
the safe default with anyone you don't know, and the only form for a group.
spoken French leaves it at the end: tu veux quoi ? Fronted it becomes qu'est-ce que: qu'est-ce que tu veux ?
vous êtes anglais ? The liaison sounds like 'voo-zet'.
je suis, shortened to 'chuis' in fast speech.
il/elle for people, and for objects according to their gender: la voiture ? elle est devant. ça takes over for a situation or an unnamed thing: ça marche, ça m'énerve.
the workhorse pronoun: ça va, c'est ça, ça marche. Before a noun use ce/cette: ce train, cette rue.
possession runs backwards: la voiture de Marie = Marie's car. de + le = du, de + les = des.
dans le sac. But countries, regions and months take en: en France, en mai.
à Paris, à la maison, à huit heures. French has no object marker like ko.

The preposition with no English equivalent, and French uses it constantly: chez ma sœur, chez le médecin, chez moi. Always chez + a person or a trade, never a place: chez le boulanger, but à la boulangerie.
sur la table, sur le mur. Also does 'about': un livre sur la France. For 'on' a day, French uses no preposition at all: on se voit lundi.
never liaises – 'et' stays 'ay' even before a vowel.
opens a sentence like to: alors, on y va ? donc is the logical 'therefore'.
this is THE spoken word for 'we', and it takes a singular verb: on y va, on mange, on est fatigués. nous belongs to writing and speeches.
family, friends, children and animals. Often heard as t' : t'as, t'es.
tu es, said 't'es' almost always: t'es prêt ?
obligatory on entering any shop. salut is the casual hello/bye; bonsoir from about six o'clock.
ça marche and OK are just as everyday.
ah bon ? = oh really? bon also opens a sentence like 'right then': bon, on y va.
goes after the verb or at the end: moi aussi.
je fais, tu fais, on fait, vous faites, ils font. Covers cooking (faire à manger) and weather (il fait chaud).
also the auxiliary for come/go verbs in the past: je suis allé.
je vais, tu vas, on va, vous allez, ils vont. Also builds the everyday future.
je viens, on vient, vous venez. venir de + infinitive = to have just done something.

items.en: present tense of -er verbs: je parle, tu parles, on parle
items.note: four of the six endings sound identical – parle, parles, parle, parlent are all 'parl'. One present covers 'I speak' and 'I'm speaking'.
picks its form from the thing owned: mon frère, ma sœur, mes parents. mon before a feminine noun starting with a vowel: mon amie.
votre for one thing, vos for several: votre fils, vos enfants.
me sits before the verb (il me donne ça); moi stands alone or after a preposition (pour moi, avec moi, moi aussi).
same word as the subject, just placed before the verb: je vous appelle demain.
c'est qui ? = who is it? Also the relative 'who/that': le monsieur qui parle.
spoken French parks it at the end: t'es où ? tu vas où ?
c'est quand ? Note the -d links as a 't': quand est-ce que.
answer with parce que.
also 'what?' when you didn't catch something: comment ?
c'est combien ? combien de personnes ? – always combien de before a noun.
viens ici. In speech là often takes over: je suis là = I'm here.
does both jobs; là-bas is 'over there', properly distant.
maintenant on y va.
j'arrive tout de suite. For 'just now' in the past: je viens d'arriver.
note the apostrophe; it's one word.
French splits what kal does with one word: demain forward, hier back. à demain = see you tomorrow.
et puis is how it's usually said. ensuite is the tidier version.
très goes with adjectives (très bon), beaucoup with verbs and nouns (j'aime beaucoup, beaucoup de monde). Never 'très beaucoup'.
un peu de sel; un petit peu softens it further.
c'est trop cher. In young speech trop also means 'really': c'est trop bien.
moins cher; for 'not much' say pas beaucoup.
ends an order at a counter. ça suffit is the firmer 'that's enough'.
singular verb: tout le monde est là. Also il y a du monde = it's busy.

items.en: some (the partitive): du pain, de la viande, des légumes
items.note: French cannot leave it out the way English drops 'some': je veux du pain, never 'je veux pain'. After a negative it flattens to de: je veux pas de pain. This is the single biggest French habit to build early.
and quelque chose = something.
always plural. du monde is the everyday alternative: il y avait du monde.
spoken French's all-purpose noun: c'est quoi ce truc ? j'ai un truc à faire. Learn it early – you'll hear it constantly.
le boulot is what people actually say: je vais au boulot.
for 'home' French prefers chez moi / chez nous: je rentre chez moi.
le prénom is the first name – that's usually what someone is asking for.
feminine: de l'eau fraîche. In a café ask for une carafe d'eau – tap water, free.
as a British learner expect disappointment; le café is the social default in France.
je mange, on mange, vous mangez. 'Food' is à manger (qu'est-ce qu'il y a à manger ?) or la nourriture.
masculine. la monnaie = change (coins).
j'ai pas le temps. For clock time it's l'heure, and une fois for 'a time/occasion'.
the neutral word; un truc is what people say out loud, quelque chose for 'something'.
un bel endroit. Careful: une place is a seat or a square, not 'a place' in general.
donner quelque chose à quelqu'un: je donne ça à Marie.
je prends, on prend, vous prenez. Ordering runs on it: je prends un café.
voir is what happens to your eyes, regarder is what you choose to look at: je vois la mer, je regarde la télé.
same split as voir/regarder: j'entends du bruit, j'écoute la radio.
no article with a language: je parle français.
je dis, tu dis, on dit, vous dites, ils disent. dis-moi = tell me.
for meeting up French says se voir or se retrouver: on se voit demain ?
je sais, tu sais, on sait, vous savez. savoir + verb = to know how: je sais nager.
je connais ta sœur, je connais Lyon. Never savoir for people.
built on prendre: je comprends, on comprend, vous comprenez.
j'habite à Londres = I live in London; je reste ici = I'm staying here.
never changes person: il faut y aller = we/you/I must go. For 'I need X' it's j'ai besoin de.
je bois, on boit, vous buvez, ils boivent.
ça marche does double duty as 'it works' and 'sounds good'.
for cooking, faire does most of the work: faire à manger, faire un gâteau.
je mets, on met, vous mettez. garder = to keep.

items.en: imperative: tu-form (no -s on -er verbs) and the polite vous-form
items.note: just drop the pronoun: (tu) viens → viens !, (vous) venez → venez !. -er verbs lose the -s: tu parles → parle !
allez ! on its own = come on! The little y means 'there' and never disappears: j'y vais.
entrez, je vous en prie is the warm full version.
assieds-toi with tu. Reflexive: you 'seat yourself'.
tiens with tu. Handing something over is tenez; putting it down in front of someone is voilà.
dis-moi with tu. je vous écoute is the shopkeeper's version.
excuse-moi with tu. The all-purpose opener before asking a stranger anything.
a woman says désolée (sounds the same). je suis vraiment désolé for a real apology.
s'il te plaît with tu. Leaving it off sounds genuinely rude in a shop.
pas de souci is the other everyday one. de rien answers merci.
French politeness rides on adding madame/monsieur rather than a particle: oui monsieur, merci madame.
the polite refusal; a bare non sounds blunt.
the universal one. comment allez-vous ? is formal and comparatively rare in speech.
the same two words answer the question. ça va bien for a bit more warmth.
et toi ? with tu.
past: qu'est-ce qui s'est passé ? For 'what's wrong?' say qu'est-ce qu'il y a ?
how it's really said. qu'est-ce que c'est ? is the tidy written order.
literally 'I call myself'. Two l's in appelle.
tu t'appelles comment ? with tu. The doubled vous vous is correct, not a typo.
French 'has' its states rather than 'being' them: j'ai faim, j'ai soif, j'ai froid, j'ai peur.
the standard line for leaving. bon, je dois y aller softens it.
mais oui / mais non add emphatic warmth: 'well of course'.
no accent, unlike où (where) – they sound identical.
parce qu'il pleut. Never starts an answer with 'car' in speech.
the everyday hesitation opener: ben oui, ben non, ben je sais pas. To call out to someone it's eh ! or oh !
every noun is masculine or feminine, so learn it with its article: un livre, une table, le pain, la voiture. Getting the gender in from day one saves years.
'seess' alone, 'see' before a consonant: six pains.
the p is silent: 'set'.
also means 'brand new'.
'deess' alone, 'dee' before a consonant: dix minutes.
what you call her when talking about her to other people.
mon père when talking about him to others.
French doesn't mark older or younger; add grand or petit if you need to.
the œ is one letter; typed oe at a pinch.
pronounced 'feess' – the l is silent.
the same word means 'girl'; context sorts it out.
describes birth order only – French has no didi-style term for addressing an older woman. To address one you use madame or her first name.
same as grande sœur: a description, never a form of address.
the obligatory French table ritual, said before anyone starts eating, even to strangers at the next café table. French has no 'have you eaten?' greeting; this is the food ritual you actually need.
no article after parler: parle français, not 'parle le français'.
or just plus lentement, s'il vous plaît. The single most useful sentence in week one.
a bare comment ? also works but sounds abrupt.
ah d'accord is the everyday 'ah, right, I see'.
the full form is je n'ai pas compris; spoken French drops the ne almost every time.

items.word: ça se dit comment en français ?
items.roman: ca se dit comment en francais ?
items.en: how do you say this in French?
items.note: or comment on dit ... en français ? Both are everyday.
lower-case f for the language and the adjective; capital F only for a French person: un Français.
c'est pour moi. pour + infinitive = in order to: pour aller à la gare ?
avec moi, avec toi – stressed pronouns after it, never je/tu.
French possession is a verb, not a 'near me' phrase: j'ai deux enfants. j'ai, t'as, il a, on a, vous avez, ils ont. Also the main past auxiliary.
je peux, tu peux, on peut, vous pouvez, ils peuvent. je peux ? on its own = may I?
vite is speed (viens vite !), bientôt is soon, tôt is early. The adjective is rapide: un train rapide, mais il va vite.
il est trois heures. One o'clock is une heure, not 'un heure'. Timetables use the 24-hour clock: dix-huit heures.
copain/copine is the everyday word; un ami is a shade more serious. Watch out: mon copain also means boyfriend.
the French counterpart of calling any older woman 'aunty': you address every adult woman as madame. ma tante is only a real aunt.
pronounced 'muh-syuh'. Add it to greetings: bonjour monsieur, merci monsieur.
toute la famille = the whole family.
the ç keeps the s sound; don't use it to call a waiter, that's long dead.
also 'daughter'.
h silent: 'un-omm'. un mec is the spoken word, un type is a bit dismissive.
pronounced 'fam'. Same word means 'wife': ma femme.
apporter for things, amener for people: j'apporte le dessert, j'amène ma sœur.
j'ouvre, on ouvre, vous ouvrez – it takes -er endings despite the -ir.
fermer la porte, but éteindre la lumière for switching things off.
le téléphone on its own suggests the landline. le portable also means a laptop – context decides.
phone only. Saying allô to someone's face is a giveaway that you learned French from a textbook.
je t'appelle ce soir. Also passer un coup de fil = to give someone a ring.

items.en: to chat, to talk things over
items.note: on a discuté = we had a chat. It doesn't imply an argument the way English 'discuss' can.
une baguette is the default loaf; un pain is a bigger, denser one.
silent z.
replaces dal as the weekday staple: this is what actually turns up on a French family table. les lentilles exist but are occasional.
masculine plural, despite the -e.
un café au lait is a breakfast drink; after a meal order un café.
tu peux me passer le sel ? le poivre = pepper.
rarely needed – French home cooking almost never is. piquant is the word for chilli heat; fort for a strong mustard or cheese.
le p'tit-déj in speech. le déjeuner is lunch and le dîner is dinner – don't be caught out by the overlap.
vous en voulez encore ? with vous. The little en means 'of it' and cannot be dropped.
c'est très bon is said far more often and lands just as well.
avoir again, not être.
en voiture = by car. la bagnole and la caisse are slang.
chambre is specifically for sleeping; une pièce is a room in general, une salle a public one.
always plural, and this is what you ask for. la salle de bains is where the bath is and may well not contain a loo.
dix euros; the s is silent. Prices are often said as 'dix euros cinquante'.
c'est combien ? is shorter and just as common.
attends with tu. arrêtez = stop (an action).
one of the few adjectives that goes before the noun: une grande maison.
also before the noun, and used constantly to soften: un petit café, un petit peu.
peut-être que oui, peut-être que non.
Literally 'it pleases me', so the thing liked is the subject and it agrees: ce film me plaît, ces chaussures me plaisent. Past: ça m'a plu.
Softens a request: je voulais juste demander. Also means fair or correct (c'est juste) and tight, of clothes.
en France = in or to France. Countries take an article: la France, l'Angleterre.
vous parlez anglais ? – no article after parler.
mes affaires = my things. les bagages / les valises for luggage.

items.word: je suis / tu es / il est / on est / vous êtes / ils sont
items.roman: je suis / tu es / il est / on est / vous etes / ils sont
items.en: present of être: am, are, is
items.note: on est, not 'on sont' – on always takes the il/elle form even though it means 'we'.
question, answer and 'that's fine' all at once: ça va ? – ça va. ça va comme ça = that's enough, thanks.
careful: merci on its own in answer to an offer usually means 'no thanks'. Say oui, merci if you want it.
sers-toi with tu. The host's line at a French table.
the polite default for ordering and asking. je veux is blunt to the point of rude. j'ai besoin de = I need.
j'aime bien = I like; j'aime on its own about a person means love. adorer for enthusiasm about things.
oui, je sais. For 'I know him' it's je le connais.
often crushed to 'chais pas'. aucune idée = no idea.
here the article stays, because the verb isn't parler: j'apprends le français.
rising intonation is all you need – no est-ce que required.
tu viens d'où ? with tu. The tidy version is d'où venez-vous ?
je suis anglais / anglaise also works. Say britannique if you'd rather not say England.
the spoken shape. où sont les toilettes ? is the tidy one.
spoken French flips it: la gare, c'est où ?
on the phone; in the family you'd just say c'est Tom.
un instant is slightly more formal; ne quittez pas on the phone.
au secours ! is the shout in a real emergency.
salut works as both hello and bye with friends; à plus (written à+) = see you.
the standard French sign-off after au revoir. bonne soirée in the evening, bon courage if they've got a hard day ahead.
the French offer is coffee, not tea. tu prends quelque chose ? covers any drink.
une enfant for a girl, but the word itself doesn't change.
les frites = chips, la purée = mash.

items.en: two-level politeness: tu with family, close friends and children; vous with everyone else and with any group
items.note: Two rungs only, and getting it wrong is the mistake people notice. Default to vous with any adult stranger and wait to be offered tu: on peut se tutoyer ?
merci bien can sound sarcastic depending on tone; beaucoup is safe.
the standard order; c'est quoi ? is the everyday spoken one.
encore une fois = one more time; encore du pain = more bread; il est encore là = he's still there.
tag it on the end: c'est bon, non ? hein ? is the very spoken version. n'est-ce pas ? is textbook-only and nobody says it.
the dish adjustment you actually need in France, in place of 'not too spicy': saignant (rare), à point (medium), bien cuit (well done).
feminine. au secours ! is the shout; à l'aide ! is more literary.
spoken order. quelle heure est-il ? is the formal inversion.
what you call her to her face, and within the family.

items.en: respect goes on the title plus the surname
items.note: the nearest thing to ji: monsieur/madame attaches to the surname, never the first name. And a bare bonjour sounds curt – bonjour madame is the polite minimum.
only ever appears in avoir faim; never 'je suis faim'.
j'ai, t'as, il a, on a. t'as is how tu as is really pronounced: t'as l'heure ?
full form il n'y a pas; spoken French drops the ne, and often the whole thing lands as 'y a pas'. c'est pas = it isn't.
point and say celui-là for a masculine thing, celle-là for a feminine one. Essential at a market stall.
écoutez with vous. Opens a point rather than an order: écoute, c'est compliqué.
never optional the way English drops 'that': je pense qu'il vient, not 'je pense il vient'.
tacked on the end for agreement or softening: c'est bon, hein ? Also a blunt 'what?' if you didn't hear.

items.en: to be in the middle of doing: je suis en train de manger
items.note: French usually needs nothing at all – je mange covers both 'I eat' and 'I'm eating'. Use en train de only when the ongoing-ness is the point.

items.word: j'étais / tu étais / il était / on était / vous étiez / ils étaient
items.roman: j'etais / tu etais / il etait / on etait / vous etiez / ils etaient
items.note: c'était is the single most useful past form in the language: c'était bien, c'était bon, c'était comment ?
agrees with the thing owned, not the owner, so sa voiture is 'his car' or 'her car' depending on context. This trips English speakers up constantly.
stays notre even when the subject is on: on prend notre voiture.
agrees with its noun: quel âge ? quelle heure ? quels enfants ?
Stands alone, without a noun: – Il y a deux trains. – Lequel je prends ? Agrees: lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles.
la journée when you mean the stretch of it: bonne journée, toute la journée.
raconte ! = go on, tell me. For 'tell me something' it's dis-moi.
false friend: it's 'ask', not 'demand'. poser une question = to ask a question.
il a l'air fatigué = he looks tired. ça m'a l'air bien = that looks good to me.
je dors, on dort, vous dormez. se coucher = to go to bed.
reflexive – you seat yourself: je m'assieds, assieds-toi, asseyez-vous.
je me lève à sept heures. The accent moves: lever → je me lève.

items.en: not; don't – negation wraps around the verb
items.note: re-tiered to day one: French negates with two pieces, je ne sais pas, and in speech the ne simply vanishes – je sais pas, c'est pas ça, fais pas ça. Learn to hear the missing half.
blunt on its own; je voudrais or vous pouvez me donner ... is what you'd normally say in a shop.
squeezing past someone, catching a stranger's attention, or asking them to repeat. s'il vous plaît ! is how you flag a waiter.
letters, officials, formal occasions. merci does everything in ordinary speech.
ça se passe bien ? for 'is it going okay?'
casual, between friends. ça roule ? is very familiar indeed.
bien actually weakens it: j'aime bien = I like, j'aime = I love. Counter-intuitive but consistent.
si + present: si tu veux, on y va. Shortens before il: s'il pleut. Same spelling as the contradicting 'yes'.
the everyday self-correction filler: c'est bon, enfin, je crois. c'est-à-dire = that is to say; ça veut dire quoi ? = what does that mean?

items.en: emphasis by doubling the subject: moi, je préfère ça
items.note: French has no emphasis particle like hi, so it repeats the subject instead: moi je sais pas, lui il vient pas. The other tool is a cleft: c'est moi qui l'ai fait.
French doesn't need a reflexive possessive – son/sa already refers back to the subject. propre only adds emphasis: il a sa propre voiture.

items.en: adjectives agree in gender and number
items.note: re-tiered to day one: every adjective agrees, and most sit after the noun (une voiture rouge). Only a short common set goes in front: bon, grand, petit, jeune, vieux, beau, nouveau.
à plus (written à+) is the casual one; à demain, à lundi, à tout à l'heure for later today.
prenez soin de vous with vous. Warm rather than routine – bonne journée is the everyday sign-off.
jusqu'à demain, jusqu'à la gare. Contracts with le: jusqu'au marché.

items.en: past tense: avoir + participle, but être with go/come-type verbs, and then it agrees
items.note: re-tiered up – you need the past within the first fortnight, and it's the only past used in speech. être verbs: aller, venir, partir, arriver, rester, entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, tomber, naître, mourir, plus every reflexive (je me suis levé).

items.en: future: je vais manger, on va y aller
items.note: aller + verb is what people actually say for anything ahead. The one-word future (je mangerai) is more distant or formal – learn it later.

items.word: à + le = au / à + les = aux / de + le = du / de + les = des
items.roman: a + le = au / a + les = aux / de + le = du / de + les = des
items.en: prepositions fuse with le and les
items.note: It is the article that changes shape, not the noun: je vais au marché, la clé du garage, je parle aux enfants. à la and de la stay separate.
on + question intonation does the job of the Hindi subjunctive: on mange ? on se voit demain ? For permission, je peux ? The real subjonctif (il faut que je fasse) comes much later.

items.en: the one belonging to / the one that
items.note: celui de Marie = Marie's one; celle qui est là = the one that's over there. Agrees: celui, celle, ceux, celles.
plus grand que moi. bon goes irregular: meilleur que, never 'plus bon'.
le plus grand, la plus belle – the article agrees. le meilleur = the best.
enormously versatile: it's tasty, it's ready, it's sorted, that's enough. c'est fait = it's been done.
je trouve que ... for a judgement about how something is; je crois que ... for a belief.
je dois y aller is the firmer 'I have to go' and the usual line for leaving a gathering.
note the partitive de l'. In a restaurant, une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît gets you free tap water.
avant, c'était mieux. d'abord = firstly, first of all.
à tout à l'heure = see you later today; à plus tard is the goodbye version.
après le repas; et après ? = and then what?
avant de partir, before a verb; plain avant before a noun: avant le dîner.
the second sense is everywhere: il est toujours là = he's still here.
des fois is the spoken one; parfois is neutral, quelquefois a bit tidier.
pairs with ne in writing (je ne vais jamais là-bas) but stands alone in speech: j'y vais jamais.
the s of tous is pronounced here: 'tooss'.
always singular: chaque jour, chaque fois. For habits, tous les jours is more natural.
l'autre = the other one; deuxième = second in a sequence.
j'ai rien vu. de rien is the standard answer to merci.
j'ai tout mangé. tous (pronounced 'tooss' as a pronoun) = all of them.
on mange à quelle heure ? – spoken French leaves the question word at the end.
same word as 'o'clock'. une demi-heure = half an hour.
dans cinq minutes.

items.roman: le premier mai, le deux mai, le quinze août
items.en: dates: ordinal for the 1st, plain numbers after
items.note: Same rule as Hindi. Both le 1er mai and le 15 août are public holidays and everything shuts
Months are lowercase; 'en janvier' = in January
The s is pronounced
Full of public holidays and long weekends
Said 'oute'; half the country is on holiday and small shops close for weeks
'la rentrée' in early September is a national event, not just a school term
Very common in France, where plenty of long-term couples never marry; 'mon copain / ma copine' for younger couples, 'mon mec / ma meuf' is slang
'ils sont fiancés'; the PACS is the everyday civil alternative to marriage
le marié / la mariée singular; 'le mariage' means both the wedding and the marriage
The respectful term; 'les anciens' in a village. Avoid calling someone 'vieux' to their face
'vieux / vieille' is blunter but very common: 'ma vieille voiture'
'faire des heures de ménage'; 'la nounou' is the childminder
Say the s in the singular (oss) but not in the plural (les os sounds like 'lay-oh')
Of chocolate, coffee and endives
'goûte ça !' = try this. 'Le goûter' as a noun is the children's afternoon snack, at about four
Still used at markets: 'une livre de tomates' = 500 g. Nothing to do with the pound sterling, which is 'une livre sterling'
'les plaques' for the whole hob; le four = oven; la gazinière = gas cooker
Bring your own: free plastic bags are banned. 'un cabas' is the sturdy market bag
'le chauffage' = the heating in general; French flats often have shared building heating
Also 'le ballon d'eau chaude'; 'la chaudière' is the boiler that does the heating too
'la transpiration'; in speech people just say 'j'ai trop chaud'

items.en: to go up; to get on
items.note: 'monter dans le bus / le train'; its opposite is descendre, which is also how you get off
The first thing said in a French household in the morning, after bonjour. Answer: 'très bien, merci'
Only when someone is actually going to bed; 'bonsoir' is what you say arriving in the evening

items.en: would you like something to drink?
items.note: The host's opening offer; 'je te sers quoi ?' once the bottles are out
'ça fait un bail' is the very spoken version; 'ça fait plaisir de te voir'
Clipped from 'ne t'inquiète pas' and heard far more often than the full form; 'pas de souci' does the same job
Back to front compared with English: the person you miss is the subject. 'ma famille me manque' = I miss my family
'je suis pris' = I'm tied up; 'je suis débordé' = I'm swamped
Short for disponible: 't'es dispo demain ?'. 'libre' works too
The spoken default: 'ça va, le boulot ?'. 'le travail' is neutral, 'un job' is a casual one
'il fait ses études à Lyon'; 'les devoirs' = homework
Spoken form of la faculté. Careful: 'le collège' is secondary school for 11 to 15 year olds and 'le lycée' is sixth form
'une émission' = a programme; 'un feuilleton' = a soap
'on regarde le match ?'; football and rugby are the family-sofa sports
'les infos de 20 heures' is a national fixture; 'les actualités' is the formal word
'aller aux urgences'. This is the word you actually need in a crisis, more than hôpital
Plural 'les genoux' with an x; 'j'ai mal aux genoux'
'tiens !' = here, take this, and you'll hear it constantly. 'tiens ?' on its own = oh, really?
Takes être in the past: 'il est tombé'. 'tomber malade' = to fall ill
'je t'offre un verre'; 'offrir' also means to give as a present

items.word: n'importe quoi / n'importe qui / n'importe où
items.roman: n'importe quoi / n'importe qui / n'importe où
items.note: 'n'importe quoi !' on its own means 'that's rubbish!' and is very common
devoir carries the guess: 'elle doit être en route', 'ça doit coûter cher'. Not derivable from its 'have to' meaning

items.en: to be in the middle of doing: je suis en train de manger
items.note: French has no -ing tense, so this is how you say what is happening right now. For 'about to', use 'je suis sur le point de' or just 'je vais partir'
'mange comme il faut'; 'bien' is the everyday adverb: 'range bien tes affaires'
The French host's line, offered and re-offered; 'tu restes dîner ?' in the evening

items.en: ring me when you get there
items.note: quand about the future takes the future in French, the same rule as hs-0368 and hs-0749: appelle-moi quand tu arriveras. You will hear the present in fast speech, but as written this item taught the opposite of the other two.
'c'est bien !' to a child; 'bien joué' after a good move or a bit of luck
'qu'il est mignon !' about a child; 'c'est gentil' about a kind gesture
'les pantoufles' is the same thing; 'les tongs' are flip-flops. Unlike India, many French homes keep shoes on, so wait and see
Everything shuts. May has several; 'faire le pont' means taking the bridging day off when one falls on a Tuesday or Thursday
French people carry 'la carte d'identité' instead, and will ask you for 'une pièce d'identité'
je me sers de mon portable pour ça. utiliser is the neutral verb; se servir de is what people say out loud.
Family video calls; 'je te mets sur haut-parleur'
'anniversaire' alone means birthday; the wedding one needs the full phrase
Always plural; 'les lunettes de soleil' = sunglasses. 'où sont mes lunettes ?' is a household classic

The syllabus teaches the negative (il y a pas) at tier 1 but never the positive. il y a du monde, il y a un problème, il y a une pharmacie ici ? Said 'y a' in speech. The same words also mean 'ago' after a time: il y a deux ans.

items.en: this; that (before a noun): ce train, cette rue, ces gens
items.note: Currently buried in a note under ça. cet before a vowel: cet homme, cet été. Add -là when you need to be clear which one: ce train-là.

items.en: the definite article, kept where English drops it
items.note: French keeps the article for generalities, days and body parts: j'aime le fromage, le lundi je travaille, la France, j'ai mal à la tête, elle a les cheveux courts. Leaving it out is one of the commonest English mistakes.
y a plus de pain = there's no bread left; j'ai plus faim = I'm not hungry any more. The s is silent here but pronounced in plus = more, and that one letter is the whole difference.
You can get by on rising intonation, but you must recognise this: est-ce que vous avez du pain ? It combines into qu'est-ce que, qu'est-ce qui, où est-ce que, quand est-ce que.

items.word: je me / tu te / il se / on se / vous vous
items.roman: je me / tu te / il se / on se / vous vous
items.en: reflexive verbs: je me lève, tu te reposes, on se voit demain
items.note: The pronoun changes with the subject and sits before the verb. It also carries 'each other': on se voit, on s'appelle. Every reflexive takes être in the past: je me suis levé.

Currently only mentioned inside another item's note. It hands something over, closes a point, agrees and fills gaps: voilà votre monnaie ; c'est ça, voilà. With bon and alors it holds spoken French together.
The standard answer to merci, and it is expected. je vous en prie is the polite version, pas de souci and avec plaisir the everyday ones.
Replaces bonjour from about six o'clock, and it is a greeting on arriving, not a farewell. bonne soirée is the one you leave on.
Hello and goodbye in one word, but only with people you would call tu. To a shopkeeper it is always bonjour.
The syllabus calls it ubiquitous in a note but never teaches it. du coup, on y va ? You will hear it every few sentences; donc is its tidier written cousin.
The commonest surprise noise in the language, and the thing you say to keep someone talking. ah d'accord = ah, I see.
Answers ça va ? without gushing, and also means a fair amount: il y a pas mal de monde.
The everyday verdict on people, places and evenings alike: il est sympa, c'était sympa. Short for sympathique, which nobody says out loud.
c'est vraiment bien ; vraiment ? ; je suis vraiment désolé. Appears only inside other notes at present.
ça dépend des jours. Buys thinking time without committing you to anything.
le même sac = the same bag ; même pas = not even ; quand même = even so. One small word doing three jobs.
pendant les vacances, pendant deux heures. Keep it apart from depuis (for, still going on) and dans (in, counting forward).
j'ai que dix euros = I've only got ten euros. It looks like a negative and isn't; seulement is the plainer alternative.

items.en: linking a silent final consonant onto the next word: vous_avez, les_enfants, deux_ans
items.note: s and x link as 'z', d as 't' (quand il vient), f as 'v' (neuf heures). Never after et. This is why spoken French sounds like one long word rather than separate ones.
Fine with family and friends, careless-sounding with anyone you would call vous. mouais = yeah, not convinced.
Missing entirely from the syllabus. je paie (or je paye), on paie, vous payez. je peux payer par carte ? ; payer en liquide ; c'est moi qui paie = it's on me.

items.en: to go back home; to get in
items.note: Not just re-entering: je rentre à quelle heure ? ; il rentre du boulot ; on rentre demain. Takes être in the past: je suis rentré tard.
je trouve pas mes clés ; tu trouves ça cher ? ; je trouve que c'est trop loin. The 'reckon' sense is as common as the 'find' one.
je choisis, on choisit, vous choisissez. t'as choisi ? is what you get asked over a menu.
The weekly food shop: je fais les courses, on va au supermarché. Different from le shopping (clothes) and from faire le marché (the outdoor market).
The daily errand, and no French deck should leave it in a footnote. la boucherie for meat, la pâtisserie for cakes, le tabac for stamps. chez le boulanger works just as well.
Any appointment, not a romantic one: j'ai rendez-vous chez le médecin à trois heures. No article after avoir: avoir rendez-vous. prendre rendez-vous = to book one.
Unavoidable in family houses and in any conversation with a child: il est à vous, le chien ? ; il s'appelle comment ?
faire sa valise = to pack. les bagages is the collective, un sac à dos a rucksack, la consigne the left-luggage office.
Masculine. Old French buildings often have none, hence par l'escalier. l'ascenseur est en panne is a sign you will meet.
on mange dans le jardin. la terrasse is the paved bit, and the same word covers a café's pavement seating.
The three courses, and how a set price is described: entrée + plat, or plat + dessert. Careful: an entrée is the starter, never the main. le plat du jour is the day's special.

items.word: une table pour deux, s'il vous plaît
items.roman: une table pour deux, s'il vous plaît
items.note: vous avez une table ? works too. In the evening ring ahead: j'ai réservé au nom de ...
Absent from a syllabus that teaches wine, coffee and lemon squash. une pression is draught; un demi is the 25cl glass you get by default; une pinte if you want a British-sized one.
What the bakery or café asks you. Answer sur place, or c'est à emporter.
Included by law, so there is no tipping arithmetic in France. Rounding up or leaving a couple of euros (un pourboire) is a bonus, never an obligation.
on s'installe en terrasse ? You may be asked salle ou terrasse ? on walking in. Sitting outside is the default in decent weather.
un aller-retour pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît. un aller simple is a single, en seconde standard class. Buying a train ticket is core travel and the syllabus has no word for it.
On every exit sign and every metro corridor: sortie 3. l'entrée is the way in, which is also the word for a starter.
je peux me garer où ? le parking is the car park, une place the space, l'horodateur the ticket machine for blue-lined bays.
Paid by card at the barrier on most autoroutes. faire le plein = to fill up ; le gazole is diesel, le sans-plomb 95 unleaded. Nothing in the syllabus covers driving in France.

items.word: pour aller à la gare, s'il vous plaît ?
items.roman: pour aller à la gare, s'il vous plaît ?
items.en: how do I get to the station, please?
items.note: The standard way to ask directions, and it needs no verb at all: pour aller à + place. Swap in la poste, la plage, le centre-ville. Currently hidden in a note under pour.
perdue if you're a woman, identical sound. je cherche cette adresse, with the phone held up, does the rest.
j'ai quarante ans. Age is something you have, and the ans can never be dropped. Fine with children and close family; as nosy as in English with an adult.
The shout in a genuine emergency; aidez-moi for anything less. 112 reaches emergency services in English anywhere in France.
The syllabus teaches only the past (j'ai pas compris). This is the one you need in the moment: je comprends pas, désolé. Written je ne comprends pas.
on va à la plage. la mer for the sea, la montagne for the other kind of French holiday.
Half of French sightseeing. la visite = the guided tour, les horaires = opening times, l'entrée = the admission fee and the way in.
en automne. Completes a set the syllabus leaves broken: le printemps (au printemps, the odd one out), l'été, l'automne, l'hiver.

items.word: un mail / le week-end / un parking
items.roman: un mail / le week-end / un parking
items.en: English loanwords that are ordinary French
items.note: French borrows freely and pronounces it its own way: un mail, un texto, le week-end, un parking, un job, le shopping. Some have drifted: un smoking is a dinner jacket, un baby-foot is table football, un pull a jumper.
